chapter_title: Measurement and Interpretation of Shear Strength Properties of Soil

sections.title: Fundamental Concepts of Shear Strength
sections.summary: Mohr-Coulomb criterion: s = c' + σ'tanφ' (effective stress) or s = Su (undrained, φ=0). Four strength states: peak (maximum stress), fully softened (corresponds to NC state, c'=0), post-rupture, and residual (very large displacements, c'≈0). Drained vs. undrained: short-term behavior of low-permeability clays is undrained; long-term is drained. NC clay generates positive pore pressure → Su < σ'vc. OC clay may generate negative pore pressure → enhanced short-term strength. Normalized behavior: Su/σ'vc = S × OCR^m (SHANSEP approach). Three levels of investigation (A, B, C) based on project complexity and soil conditions.
sections.body:
Mohr-Coulomb criterion: shear strength s = c' + σ'tanφ' where c' = effective cohesion and φ' = effective friction angle. For total stress undrained analysis: s = Su (φ = 0). Four strength states: (1) peak strength — maximum stress in stress-strain relationship; (2) fully softened strength — corresponds to NC state, c' = 0 (post-peak, before residual); (3) post-rupture strength — after formation of failure surface; (4) residual strength — at large displacements on pre-existing failure surfaces, c' ≈ 0.

Drained vs. undrained behavior: Low-permeability fine-grained soils may be undrained during rapid loading or construction. NC clays under undrained loading generate positive excess pore pressures, reducing effective stress and mobilized strength — Su < σ'vc. OC clays generate negative excess pore pressures, giving enhanced short-term undrained strength; this enhancement is NOT reliable for long-term design in fissured OC clays.

Normalized behavior: Su/σ'vc is a function of OCR: Su/σ'vc = S × OCR^m (SHANSEP approach) where S and m are soil-specific parameters. For many clays, S ≈ 0.25–0.30, m ≈ 0.8–0.9.

Three levels of investigation: Level A (highest) — requires undisturbed samples and advanced testing; for embankments on soft clay, bridge foundations. Level B — requires undisturbed samples and routine testing; for most routine structures. Level C (lowest) — index property measurements; for routine embankments and fills.
key_points: Mohr-Coulomb: s = c' + σ'tanφ' (drained) or s = Su (undrained φ=0)
Four strength states: peak, fully softened, post-rupture, residual — each appropriate for different conditions
NC clay: positive excess pore pressures → undrained Su < long-term drained; OC: negative → enhanced short-term
SHANSEP: Su/σ'vc = S × OCR^m; S ≈ 0.25–0.30; m ≈ 0.8–0.9 for many clays
Enhanced OC undrained strength NOT reliable long-term in fissured clays — use drained effective stress for design

sections.title: Measurement of Undrained Shear Strength
sections.summary: Undrained shear strength Su: UC test (AASHTO T208/ASTM D2166) — most common but sensitive to disturbance and desiccation; UU triaxial (AASHTO T234/ASTM D2850) — better than UC if no reconsolidation; CU-bar triaxial (ASTM D4767) — best laboratory method, gives Su and φ' simultaneously. Field vane shear (FVT/VST, ASTM D2573): correction factor μ from Chandler (1988) per PI of soil. CPT: Su = (qt-σvo)/Nkt; Nkt ≈ 12–17 typical range (site-specific calibration preferred). CPTU: Su from Bq pore pressure ratio. DMT: Su from p0-u0. Pocket penetrometer and Torvane — for screening only, not design.
sections.body:
Unconfined compression (UC) test: Simplest method; specimen sheared at constant strain rate. Su = qu/2. Subject to disturbance and desiccation effects; may substantially underestimate Su. Not recommended as primary method.

Unconsolidated undrained (UU) triaxial test (ASTM D2850): Specimen not reconsolidated prior to shear; provides Su directly but doesn't account for stress history changes. Results sensitive to sampling disturbance.

Consolidated undrained (CU-bar) triaxial test (ASTM D4767): Specimen reconsolidated to field stress state, then sheared undrained with pore pressure measurement. Preferred laboratory method; provides both Su and φ'. Various consolidation procedures: isotropic (CIUC) or anisotropic (CAU) consolidation to σ'vc.

Field vane shear test (FVT/VST, ASTM D2573): Most common in situ test for Su. Vane rotated in soft to medium clay; Su = Torque / K where K is vane constant. Correction factor μ = su,design/su,FVT per Chandler (1988), function of PI. Use μ when designing with FVT results.

CPT: Su = (qt - σvo) / Nkt where Nkt is a dimensionless cone factor. Nkt typically ranges 12–17 for most clays; best calibrated from adjacent CU triaxial tests or FVT. CPTU: Su also estimated from Bq = (u2-u0)/(qt-σvo).

DMT: Su = (p0 - u0) / (1.25 to 1.75); site-specific calibration recommended.

Torvane and pocket penetrometer: Screening tools only; not reliable for design. Significant scatter and disturbance.
key_points: CU-bar triaxial (ASTM D4767) is the preferred laboratory method — reconsolidates to field stress, measures Su and φ' simultaneously
UC test: simplest but most affected by disturbance and desiccation; not recommended as primary method
FVT (ASTM D2573): correction factor μ = su,design/su,FVT from Chandler (1988) per PI is required
CPT: Su = (qt-σvo)/Nkt; Nkt = 12–17 typical; calibrate against CU triaxial or FVT at each site
Pocket penetrometer and Torvane: screening only, not for design

sections.title: Effective Stress Strength and Special Considerations
sections.summary: Effective stress strength parameters (c', φ') from consolidated drained (CD) or consolidated undrained with pore pressure measurement (CU-bar, ASTM D4767) triaxial tests, or direct shear (ASTM D3080). φ' from SPT: Schmertmann (1975) chart; N60 → φ' function of σ'vo; for N60 > 15: φ' ≈ 28 + 0.45N60 approximately. φ' from CPT: qt-based correlations. OC stiff fissured clays: use fully softened strength (c'=0) for long-term anchored wall design; residual strength if pre-existing failure surface. Compacted soils: strength strongly dependent on compaction condition (wet vs. dry of optimum). Three considerations: peak, fully softened, and residual strength states.
sections.body:
Effective stress strength from laboratory: CD triaxial test (ASTM D7181) — most direct; slow drained shear. CU-bar triaxial (ASTM D4767) — faster; interpret effective stress envelope from total minus pore pressure. Direct shear test (ASTM D3080) — simplest; shear plane imposed; good for φ' but uncertain drainage; good for residual strength with ring shear or repeated direct shear.

φ' from SPT (indirect): Schmertmann (1975) chart (Figure 7-41) — relates φ' to N60 and σ'vo. Hatanaka and Uchida (1996) correlation. For very coarse soils requiring LPT or BPT.

φ' from CPT: qt and friction angle correlations (Figure 7-43 from Andersen and Schjetne 2013). Table 7-6: parameters for empirical φ' estimation (Duncan et al. 2014).

Strength states for stiff fissured OC clays: (1) Peak — reliable only for initial loading at low OCR; (2) Fully softened — c'=0, φ' from remolded or NC specimens; appropriate for long-term design of walls and slopes in fissured clays when no previous failure surface exists; (3) Residual — applicable if pre-existing failure surface; established by ring shear or repeated direct shear to large displacements; correlated with PI (Stark and Eid 1994).

Compacted soils: Strength depends strongly on compaction condition. Soils compacted wet of optimum have lower peak strength and less strain-softening. Soils compacted dry of optimum have higher peak but more brittleness and potential for collapse.
key_points: CD or CU-bar triaxial (ASTM D4767) preferred for c', φ'; direct shear good for φ' and residual
φ' from SPT: Schmertmann (1975) chart; φ' increases with N60 and decreases with σ'vo
Stiff fissured OC clays: use fully softened (c'=0) for design; residual if pre-existing failure surface
Residual φ' from Stark and Eid (1994) correlation with clay size fraction and LL or PI
Compacted soils: dry of optimum → higher peak, more brittle; wet of optimum → lower peak, less brittle
